extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and psychologists interested in mathematical creativity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria about how mathematical invention and understanding occur: the mental qualities, stages (conscious work, unconscious incubation, verification), and heuristics that lead to new mathematical discoveries. Useful for assessing or cultivating mathematical creativity and research practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition of mathematical order
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical demonstration is not a mere juxtaposition of syllogisms; the order in which elements are placed is more important than the elements themselves. Having the feeling or intuition of this order lets one perceive the reasoning as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This global grasp lets the mathematician avoid needing to remember every element separately: each element 'takes its allotted place' in the array. It's a key faculty for creation and for reconstructing proofs; exercises should cultivate seeing overall structure rather than only local steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and attention (reliable retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A very sure memory or prodigious force of attention allows one to retain demonstrations, rules, and intermediate propositions; without these, people make slips or forget meanings and apply rules wrongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory/attention can compensate for weaker intuition: those with strong memory can learn and apply mathematics but may not create. Rigorously recording work and checking calculations reduces errors caused by imperfect memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment/choice in invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To create is not just to make new combinations of known entities but to choose among the infinite combinations those which are useful; invention is discernment, not blind generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productive work focuses on selecting combinations that reveal mathematical laws or analogies; training should emphasize criteria for usefulness (e.g., capacity to lead to general laws) rather than combinatorial breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic sensibility as a selective sieve
rubrics_metrics.description: A special esthetic sensibility (sense of mathematical beauty, harmony, and elegance) acts as the delicate sieve that lets only the most harmonious and useful unconscious combinations reach consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical beauty correlates with usefulness: beautiful/harmonious constructs tend to reveal laws. Cultivating sensitivity to elegance helps prioritize fruitful ideas; beware that aesthetic appeal can mislead (false but elegant ideas occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the unconscious (incubation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious (subliminal) mental work plays an important role in invention: after prolonged prior work, ideas often appear suddenly during rest or unrelated activity, giving the decisive insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productive practice includes deliberate periods of conscious effort followed by rest; value incubation and allow time away from problems. Expect inspirations to arise unexpectedly but to depend on prior efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of prior conscious work
rubrics_metrics.description: Fruitful unconscious work is possible only if preceded by an extended period of voluntary, conscious effort which may appear fruitless; these efforts 'set agoing the unconscious machine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat incubation as a substitute for hard work: systematic attempts and failures prepare the subconscious by mobilizing relevant elements. Persistent, focused attempts before resting increase chance of useful unconscious recombinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of subsequent conscious verification and development
rubrics_metrics.description: After a sudden inspiration, a second period of conscious work is necessary to put ideas in shape, deduce consequences, arrange demonstrations, and verify them; inspiration alone is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inspirations as starting points; rigorously formalize, check, and compute in a conscious phase. The vivid certainty accompanying an idea can be deceptive—verification is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious mobilization of relevant elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious efforts mobilize certain 'atoms' (elements) so that during unconscious activity they are free to combine; the will does not choose atoms at random but targets ones likely to produce the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted problem-solving moves (even unsuccessful ones) are valuable because they prime the unconscious with relevant components. Design deliberate preliminary explorations aimed at mobilizing promising elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain analogies and distant combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The most fertile chosen combinations are often formed from elements drawn from domains far apart; analogies that reveal kinship between previously unrelated facts lead to important discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage exposure to diverse mathematical areas and look for analogies; rare but high-impact ideas arise from unexpected cross-domain links. Seek analogical reasoning as a heuristic for discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of purely mechanical rule application
rubrics_metrics.description: Rote application of rules without understanding leads to errors when memory fails; mathematics cannot be reduced to making all combinations mechanically—the inventor must avoid purely automatic procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize comprehension of why rules hold, not only how to apply them. Train for conceptual understanding to reduce mistakes from mechanical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious does not perform long algorithmic computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious inspiration rarely supplies the result of long, rule-bound calculations; it typically provides only a point of departure or heuristic, while detailed calculation requires conscious discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inspirations to identify routes or starting lemmas, then carry out algorithmic derivations consciously. Don't expect full algebraic verification to emerge from incubation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden illumination often reliable but fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspirations typically accompany a feeling of absolute certitude and usually are not deceivers, but sometimes the vivid feeling is mistaken and the idea fails verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the felt certainty of an insight as provisional; always subject inspirations to careful scrutiny and proof before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical understanding is selective — not universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people cannot understand higher mathematics despite shared logic rules; some lack the delicate feeling (intuition/esthetic sensibility) or sufficient memory/attention, and therefore cannot create or grasp advanced mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize individual differences: teaching and evaluation should account for varying balances of memory, attention, and intuitive sense. Development of sensibility and structure-recognition can be targets of pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and sequence matter more than isolated propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Between encountering a proposition and later using it as a premise, memory may fail or meanings shift; the preservation of the correct order and meaning is critical to avoid error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep explicit records of intermediate results and their intended meanings. When reconstructing long arguments, pay attention to how earlier conclusions function as later premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional engagement and aesthetic pleasure aid discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional sensibility (the pleasure derived from harmony and elegance) influences which unconscious products become conscious; mathematical taste helps select fruitful ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate appreciation for elegant, harmoniously ordered structures as a practical heuristic. Arousal of aesthetic response can be a signal worth investigating further, but balance with rigorous checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention is not brute-force search
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor does not examine all possible samples; many sterile combinations never even present themselves to consciousness—the creative mind avoids useless combinations rather than mechanically generating all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus efforts on principled selection heuristics rather than exhaustive enumeration. Develop criteria that filter out likely-sterile directions early (e.g., lack of analogy or aesthetic fit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write/express results to prevent semantic drift and error
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in mathematics can arise because propositions encountered earlier lose their precise meaning over time; externalizing demonstrations prevents replacing a proposition by a slightly different one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document proofs and formalisms promptly. Use writing and explicit statements to fix meanings and reduce the risk of misremembering or subtle shifts.
